strengths: Clearly formalizes an underexplored but practically important problem: group-wise counterfactual attribution for diffusion models, distinguishing it conceptually and technically from instance-level attribution (nonlinearity/non-additivity of group effects).

Provides a principled theoretical justification for using ReTrack-style redirection as an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only (LOGO) training objective in the unconditional case (Appendix A.1), rather than treating unlearning as an ad-hoc proxy.

Proposes a non-trivial extension to the conditional text-to-image setting (CLIP-weighted style-selection anchors) that correctly identifies and addresses a real failure mode of naively applying ReTrack when the forget condition is out-of-support under the retain-only prompt distribution.

Reasonably thorough empirical study across two settings (CIFAR-10 unconditional and UnlearnCanvas/SD1.5 conditional), with comparisons to multiple relevant baselines (CLIPA, TRAK, D-TRAK, DAS, ESD, Wang et al. 2024) and useful ablations on unlearning hyperparameters (epochs, forget weight, K-NN, learning rate) and gradient-method configuration (ridge regularization, aggregation strategy).
Reports both attribution accuracy and wall-clock cost, demonstrating substantial (~100x and ~5x) speedups over LOGO retraining while retaining better head-identification accuracy than baselines.
Extensive appendix detailing implementation choices, prompt construction, and evaluation metrics, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation pipeline stacks several layers of approximation: LOGOA itself is only an ELBO-based likelihood surrogate (not true log-likelihood), and in the UnlearnCanvas setting the "oracle" LOGO model is itself only a fine-tuned approximation (not from-scratch retraining) from the same checkpoint as the full model. This weakens the strength of claims about fidelity to a genuine counterfactual, since GUDA is being validated against another approximation rather than a rigorous ground truth.

Absolute performance on the more realistic conditional setting is fairly modest (45.6% Top-1 on UnlearnCanvas), which tempers claims of "reliable" identification of primary contributing groups for high-stakes use cases like copyright assessment mentioned in the introduction.

Scale and realism of experiments is limited: CIFAR-10 uses a small unconditional model with only 10 clearly separable classes, and the artistic-style experiment restricts evaluation to only 16 of 60 styles for computational reasons; it remains unclear whether the method's accuracy and speedup properties hold at the scale of real production text-to-image models with thousands of overlapping data groups and non-disjoint memberships (explicitly left as future work).

The theoretical grounding for the conditional anchor-based redirection (GUDA-C) is considerably weaker than for the unconditional case; unlike ReTrack's provable unbiased reformulation, the anchor-swap heuristic lacks a formal connection to the LOGO objective, relying instead on intuitive content-preserving/style-swapping arguments.

Key hyperparameters for GUDA-C (τ, η_mix, number of descriptors) are reported as chosen via a sweep, but no ablation results are shown for the conditional setting (unlike the extensive ReTrack/DAS ablations for CIFAR-10), leaving the sensitivity of the conditional method underexplored.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported for the main comparison tables, making it hard to assess the robustness of the reported gains over close baselines (e.g., CLIPA and DAS on CIFAR-10 are fairly close to GUDA on several metrics).

The Wang et al. (2024) baseline underperforms dramatically (4.7% Top-1, near random), which is a large gap that raises questions about whether the baseline was tuned/implemented as fairly as GUDA, especially given it was evaluated with far fewer per-style samples (20 vs. full 400) than its original design intended.

The disjoint-group assumption is a significant practical limitation for real style/copyright attribution scenarios, where artistic influences and object categories often overlap; this is acknowledged but not addressed.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: group-wise counterfactual attribution as distinct from instance-level attribution, with a precise LOGOA estimand defined via ELBO differences relative to an explicit LOGO retraining oracle.

Rare and valuable evaluation methodology: the authors actually construct LOGO oracle models (full retraining on CIFAR-10, and fine-tuning-based LOGO proxies on UnlearnCanvas/SD1.5) to serve as ground truth, enabling direct fidelity measurement rather than relying on proxy metrics alone.

Solid theoretical justification connecting the ReTrack-based unlearning objective to the retain-only (LOGO) training objective via an importance-sampling reformulation (Appendix A.1), giving some principled grounding for why unlearning approximates the counterfactual.

Thoughtful adaptation to the conditional text-to-image setting (GUDA-C) with a well-motivated anchor-construction scheme (content-preserving, style-swapping) that addresses the condition-distribution mismatch that a naive ReTrack extension would face.

Extensive ablations and robustness checks: hyperparameter sweeps for ReTrack and DAS, an ELBO-vs-probability-flow-ODE likelihood validation study, and a noisy group-partition robustness experiment, which substantially strengthen confidence in the reported trends.

Demonstrated computational advantage (∼100x on CIFAR-10, ∼5x on UnlearnCanvas) over LOGO retraining while outperforming several reasonable baselines (CLIPA, DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK, Wang et al. 2024) on head-identification metrics.

Honest and fairly detailed limitations discussion, including acknowledgment that the unlearning operator is not a certified deletion mechanism, that ELBO is an imperfect likelihood surrogate, and that the disjoint group assumption may not hold in practice.
weaknesses: Absolute attribution fidelity to the LOGO oracle remains modest in absolute terms (e.g., Top-1 agreement of 45.6% on UnlearnCanvas and 72.7% on CIFAR-10), which raises questions about practical reliability for consequential use cases like copyright assessment, despite outperforming baselines.

The LOGO oracle itself is only a true from-scratch retraining on the small CIFAR-10 setting; for UnlearnCanvas the oracle is itself a fine-tuning approximation from a shared pretrained checkpoint, so the validation against a genuine full-retraining counterfactual for large-scale text-to-image models is not actually demonstrated.

Evaluation scale is limited (10 CIFAR-10 classes, and only 16 of 60 UnlearnCanvas styles), leaving open how well the approach and its claimed speedups generalize to attribution settings with hundreds or thousands of groups (e.g., many individual artists), which is the primary practical motivation of the paper.

The framework fundamentally requires per-group unlearning (cost scaling linearly in N), so while it is much cheaper than retraining, it does not fully resolve the scalability bottleneck for very large numbers of groups; this trade-off is not empirically explored at larger N.

The core unlearning operator (ReTrack) is adopted from prior work rather than newly proposed, and no formal bound is given on the approximation error between the unlearning-based counterfactual and the true LOGO counterfactual—reliance is entirely on empirical validation in the two studied settings.

The disjoint, non-overlapping group partition assumption is a significant practical limitation (styles and concepts often overlap or blend), and while a small-scale noisy-partition robustness check is included, it only tests 5% random membership noise rather than genuinely overlapping/hierarchical groupings.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably thorough, involve reimplementations of prior methods (D-TRAK, TRAK, DAS, Wang et al.) whose hyperparameters may not be fully optimized for this specific group-attribution task despite the ablations provided, leaving some uncertainty about baseline competitiveness.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper carefully distinguishes group-wise counterfactual attribution from instance-level attribution and grounds it in an explicit LOGO-style estimand (Eq. 4), which is a useful conceptual contribution.

The theoretical derivation connecting ReTrack-style redirection to an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only training objective (Appendix A.1) gives some principled justification for using unlearning as a LOGO proxy, rather than treating unlearning as an ad hoc heuristic.

Extensive ablations (K-NN truncation, learning rate, epochs, forget-loss weight, aggregation strategies for baselines, anchor-selection strategy) and a sanity check comparing the ELBO surrogate against a PF-ODE likelihood oracle (Appendix D.5) and a noisy-partition robustness test (Appendix D.6) reflect above-average empirical rigor and honest limitation reporting.

Demonstrates non-trivial wall-clock savings over LOGO retraining (~100x on CIFAR-10, ~5x on UnlearnCanvas) while outperforming several reasonable baselines (CLIPA, D-TRAK, TRAK, DAS, Wang et al.) on head-identification metrics.
weaknesses: Scale of evaluation is very limited relative to the paper's motivating claims: only 10 CIFAR-10 classes and 16 (of 60) UnlearnCanvas styles are evaluated, so the central claim that group-wise attribution is needed because LOGO 'becomes prohibitive as the number of groups grows' is never actually stress-tested at a scale where this matters; it's unclear how GUDA's per-group unlearning cost and attribution quality behave as N grows into the hundreds or thousands (e.g., real-world numbers of artists/styles).

Absolute performance is modest, especially in the more realistic text-to-image setting: GUDA achieves only 45.6% Top-1 agreement on a 16-way style attribution task, and even on the easier 10-class CIFAR-10 task Top-1 is 72.7% — useful relative improvements over baselines, but not strong enough in absolute terms to instill confidence for practical use cases like copyright/compensation decisions that the paper motivates in the introduction.

The 'oracle' itself is a fine-tuning-based LOGO proxy rather than true from-scratch retraining for the SD/UnlearnCanvas experiments (and even for CIFAR-10, LOGO retraining shares the pretrained diffusion schedule/architecture). Since GUDA and the oracle are both derived from the same fine-tuning-based paradigm, the reported fidelity may partly reflect this shared inductive bias rather than a genuinely independent validation of the counterfactual approximation.

The two instantiations (GUDA-U via ReTrack, GUDA-C via CLIP-weighted anchor redirection) are quite different, non-unified mechanisms; GUDA-C's forget loss depends on several heuristic design choices (descriptor extraction via VLM, soft-ranking filtering with hyperparameter α, CLIP-based style-selection temperature/mixing) that feel engineered post hoc for this particular benchmark rather than emerging from a principled framework, weakening the paper's claim of a coherent 'general framework.'

The ELBO-as-likelihood-surrogate assumption is only validated on CIFAR-10 (10 classes) with a Pearson correlation of 0.82 (not near 1), and Table 13 shows appreciable metric shifts under the stricter PF-ODE oracle (e.g., GUDA Top-1 drops from 0.727 to 0.645, and competitor rankings shift on some metrics), suggesting the ELBO surrogate does introduce a non-negligible source of attribution error that is not fully characterized for the more important text-to-image setting.

The comparison with Wang et al. (2024) may be somewhat unfair, since that method was designed for instance-level attribution of synthesized outputs and is merely repurposed/aggregated for group-level scoring here without clear indication that its hyperparameters were tuned for this different task, which could partly explain its near-random performance rather than reflecting a fundamental limitation of instance-level unlearning signals for group attribution.

Novelty is incremental: the core technical pieces (ReTrack unlearning, ELBO-based scoring, CLIP similarity baselines) are adopted largely from prior work, and the paper's contribution is primarily the combination/framing (LOGOA estimand + validation protocol) rather than a new algorithmic mechanism, which somewhat limits the paper's originality for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: group-wise counterfactual attribution (LOGOA) is precisely defined via ELBO differences, with LOGO retraining as an explicit oracle target, addressing a genuine gap between costly retraining-based attribution and heuristic similarity-based approaches.

Strong theoretical grounding for GUDA-U: the paper derives that the ReTrack objective is (pre-approximation) an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only training loss, giving a principled reason to expect fidelity to the LOGO counterfactual, and further justifies the K-NN truncation via exponential weight decay.

Non-trivial extension to the conditional (text-to-image) setting: the paper correctly identifies why naively applying ReTrack fails under conditioning (prompt distribution shift) and proposes a CLIP-weighted anchor redirection strategy with a matching ablation showing it outperforms simpler anchor alternatives.

Extensive and careful empirical validation: experiments on CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas/Stable Diffusion, comparisons against multiple baselines (CLIPA, DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK, Wang et al.), thorough hyperparameter ablations (Appendix D.1, D.2), a dedicated study validating the ELBO surrogate against a PF-ODE likelihood oracle, and a robustness check under noisy group partitions.

Reports concrete wall-clock costs and demonstrates substantial (~100x on CIFAR-10, ~5-18x on UnlearnCanvas) speedups over LOGO retraining and competing methods, which is directly relevant to the paper's practicality claims.

Transparent and appropriately scoped limitations and impact statement, including honest acknowledgment that the unlearning operator is not a certified deletion mechanism and that the LOGO oracle used for large-scale models is itself an approximation (fine-tuning-based, not from-scratch).
weaknesses: The 'gold standard' LOGO oracle for UnlearnCanvas is itself only a fine-tuning-based approximation (from the same SD1.5 checkpoint) rather than true from-scratch retraining, which somewhat weakens the strength of the counterfactual fidelity claims in the more realistic, large-scale setting.

Absolute attribution accuracy remains modest in the text-to-image setting (Top-1 ≈ 0.46, NDCG@3 ≈ 0.73), and the PF-ODE oracle comparison in Appendix D.5 shows a non-trivial drop in some metrics (e.g., Spearman 0.265→0.187) and DAS/D-TRAK becoming more competitive on ranking metrics under the stricter oracle, suggesting the ELBO surrogate's advantage over other methods may be somewhat overstated for full-ranking (non-head) evaluation.

The framework currently only supports disjoint, non-overlapping group partitions; the paper acknowledges this but the robustness check to overlapping/hierarchical groups is only a limited 5% noisy-reassignment test rather than a genuine overlapping-group scenario.

Evaluation is restricted to two specific settings (CIFAR-10 classes, 16 artistic styles from UnlearnCanvas with SD1.5), leaving open how well the approach scales to substantially larger, more heterogeneous group sets or other conditioning modalities/group types (e.g., copyright-relevant artist identities beyond style, demographic groups) mentioned as future work.

GUDA-C's anchor construction is fairly specific to the artistic-style use case (content/style descriptor decomposition via VLM-extracted vocabularies), and its generality to other group definitions (e.g., object categories, concepts without clean content/style separability) is not demonstrated.
